title: Eugene Onegin
facts: Eugene Onegin premiered in Moscow on 29 March 1879, conducted by Nikolai Rubinstein.
Worried about an opera without traditional scene changes, Tchaikovsky wanted maximum simplicity and sincerity, so he entrusted the premiere to Moscow Conservatory students.
Tchaikovsky didn’t call it an opera but “lyrical scenes”: selected highlights of Onegin’s life rather than a continuous story.
The idea came from the singer Yelizaveta Lavrovskaya in May 1877. After a sleepless night, Tchaikovsky embraced it.
Tchaikovsky thought Pushkin’s novel weak on plot; its strength was its characters, social commentary and beautiful verse.
The libretto keeps much of Pushkin’s own poetry from his novel in verse.
Monsieur Triquet’s verses were written by Tchaikovsky’s friend Konstantin Shilovsky.
Gustav Mahler conducted the Hamburg premiere in 1892. Tchaikovsky called him “simply a genius burning with a desire to conduct”.
The Met gave the US premiere on 24 March 1920, but its first performance in Russian came only on 15 October 1977.
Gremin’s aria “Love knows no age” is partly hummed by characters in Chekhov’s play Three Sisters.
The first performance outside Russia was in Prague in 1888, conducted by Tchaikovsky himself.
